source.title: Evaluating Concept-based Explanations of Language Models: A Study on Faithfulness and Readability
source.authors: Meng Li; Hao-Ran Jin; Ruixuan Huang; Zhihao Xu; De-Fu Lian; Zijia Lin; Di Zhang; Xi-Ting Wang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present, but some figure and table content is garbled or flattened.
record.tranche_reason: A case study reports that a concept explanation generated from limited activating examples failed to simulate the original activations, refining the claim that inspecting examples can overstate what is explained.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates readability and faithfulness of concept explanations, including neuron-based concepts. It does not audit the share of neuron poles with one or more jobs, test the classic InceptionV1 examples, examine attribution graphs, or study modern large or MoE models. The case-study failure is the direct result relevant to V6. Other reported comparisons and LLM-Score results do not establish how often neuron explanations receive good activation-prediction scores.
record.test_reason: This is a meta-evaluation of concept-explanation metrics. Bills et al.'s LLM simulation score is used only as a comparator readability measure, and its reliability is assessed. No rate of neuron explanations that fit examples but fail to predict activations is reported, and no share of well-scored neurons. The one simulation failure (Appendix D, case 3) is a single anecdote. It is not identified as a neuron rather than a sparse-autoencoder feature: case 1 matches the SAE 'directions' concept in Table 5. So it cannot bear on V6's neuron claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with additions. The authors propose perturbation-based faithfulness and coherence-based readability measures, plus a measurement-theory meta-evaluation. That evaluation filters out LLM-Score, GRAD-Loss, IN-UCI and IN-UMass for low reliability. They recommend EmbCos as a cheap substitute for human readability ratings. In a secondary comparison, SAE concepts beat neurons and TCAV beats SAE.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates concept explanations with perturbation-based faithfulness and coherence/readability measures; it does not reproduce the Qwen3 neuron-pole audit or its job-count procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report broadly consistent reliability and validity findings across tested layers and backbones, with some fluctuations and slightly better subset consistency in deeper layers.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia-70M layer 3, neuron concepts scored below SAE concepts on all readability and faithfulness measures, and SAE concepts scored below supervised TCAV.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small LMs, MLP neurons are less readable and less faithful on coherence and perturbation metrics than SAE features.

fits_no_version.finding: The LLM-Score simulation metric fell below the 0.9 test-retest reliability standard. EmbCos correlated with human readability ratings at least as well (Kendall IR 0.56 vs 0.54).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-simulation explanation scores are not test-retest reliable, which limits their use for estimating neuron interpretability shares.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The direct activation-simulation failure is a qualitative case study rather than a systematic rate. The main analysis focuses on small models, and some figure values in the supplied text are garbled.
record.rows_left_out: Other results on automatic-measure correlations, human ratings, and faithfulness-measure correlations were not extracted because they do not report the activation-prediction failure or neuron-pole job proportions in the claim.

untested.parts: Only Pythia-70M and GPT-2 small; no shares of interpretable neurons.
No architecture, regularization or tool comparison on neuron interpretability share.
No systematic test of whether example-fitting neuron explanations fail to predict activations; only one anecdote of unspecified concept type.
LLM-Score values per neuron, the share with good scores and explainer-strength comparisons are not reported. Only the metric's reliability and correlation with humans (Table 4) are given.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5 and V6 'supports' label are reversed here. The Appendix D case is one example, likely not a neuron, and its failure is attributed to a limited example budget. The models are small (70M and 124M) and the figure values are garbled.

versions.untested_parts: No audit of neuron-pole job counts or proportions, and no comparable estimate for Qwen3-32B.
No broad model-size, MoE, or trillion-parameter scaling evaluation.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car examples or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No comparison of architecture, regularization, or tool quality for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
No attribution-graph test using a large model’s own neurons.
Only a qualitative case study is reported; the paper does not systematically test explanations across neurons or quantify how often example-based explanations fail to predict activations.

The paper evaluates LLM-Score reliability and agreement with human readability ratings, but does not report the share of neurons receiving good activation-simulation scores or compare stronger explainer models on that outcome.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared an LLM-generated concept explanation and simulated activations with the original concept activation in a case study.

conditions.value: generated from a limited set of examples

rows.measure: Whether simulated activations align with the original activation
rows.value: The explanation omitted attributes beyond mathematical symbols and markup, and the simulated activations did not align with the original activation.
rows.note: The paper attributes this failure to the limited examples available to the LLM. The target model for this case is not identified in the text.
rows.check: Single qualitative case (1 of 3; the other two simulated well). The concept type is not stated and the pool mixes neuron and SAE concepts; case 1 is the SAE directions feature. The failure is blamed on too few examples, not on an explanation that fits its examples yet misses firing. No rate or score is given, so it does not measure V6's neuron effect.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Measured test-retest reliability of LLM-Score across concept explanations.

conditions.value: 100 randomly sampled concepts per unsupervised baseline in the main comparison

rows.baseline: The paper states a minimal acceptable standard of 0.9; exact LLM-Score value is not stated in the text.
rows.value: Described as less acceptable; the authors attribute this potentially to randomness in sampling highly probable tokens.
rows.note: This is a reliability result for the scoring measure, not a report of the fraction of neuron explanations with good activation-prediction scores.
rows.check: Measures the scoring metric's test-retest reliability, not how many neurons score well. The value is not legible; the text only says the score is below the 0.9 standard ('less acceptable'). The baseline field should read 0.9 standard.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared average readability and faithfulness measures for neuron-based concepts with sparse-autoencoder and TCAV concepts.

conditions.value: middle layer; main analysis uses the 3rd layer
averages across 100 randomly sampled concepts for neuron and sparse-autoencoder methods

rows.measure: Average concept readability and faithfulness across evaluated measures
rows.value: The neuron-based method was reported to be below the sparse autoencoder across all evaluated measures; exact figure values are not legible in the supplied text.
rows.note: This relative comparison does not establish the proportion of neuron poles with a single nameable job.
rows.check: Compares neuron and SAE concept averages on the study's own metrics in Pythia-70M layer 3. Gives no share of interpretable neurons, and the figure values are illegible.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
